procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 25.01.2022 passed by the learned Single Judge of the Madras High Court in CRLOP No. 1067 of 2022, granting anticipatory bail to the respondent-accused under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent-accused filed an application under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 before the Madras High Court seeking anticipatory bail in connection with an unspecified crime. The Public Prosecutor opposed the grant of anticipatory bail. The High Court allowed the application and granted anticipatory bail.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State (Appellant) appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the High Court's order, finding it to be cryptic and perverse.

directions: The impugned order is quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a case involving a commercial quantity of a narcotic substance without the court mandatorily recording the satisfaction required under Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.

facts: The case involved the recovery of a huge commercial quantity of a narcotic substance (232.5 kg of ganja).
The respondent-accused was implicated as a conspirator in the procurement and supply of the substance.
The Public Prosecutor opposed the accused's application for anticipatory bail in the High Court.
Despite the opposition and the large quantity of drugs, the High Court granted anticipatory bail to the accused.
law: Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, governs bail for offences involving commercial quantities of narcotics.
This section imposes a mandatory requirement on the court when considering bail (either regular or anticipatory) if the Public Prosecutor opposes it.

The court must record its satisfaction that there are reasonable grounds to believe two things: (1) the accused is not guilty of the offence, and (2) the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had granted anticipatory bail without mandatorily recording the satisfaction required by the conditions in Section 37 of the NDPS Act.
The High Court had completely ignored the fact that the quantity of the narcotic substance recovered was multiple times the commercial quantity.

The Court noted that in cases involving such a huge quantity of narcotics, courts should be very cautious (or "slow") in granting bail, especially anticipatory bail, and particularly when the accused has alleged criminal antecedents.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a court cannot grant anticipatory bail in a case involving a commercial quantity of a narcotic substance without first mandatorily recording its satisfaction on the twin conditions laid out in Section 37 of the NDPS Act: that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit another offence while on bail.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail was justified, despite ignoring the recovery of a narcotic substance multiple times the commercial quantity and the alleged criminal antecedents of the accused.

facts: The case involved the recovery of a very large quantity of narcotics (232.5 kg of ganja), which is multiple times the commercial quantity.
The accused was alleged to be a conspirator in the procurement and supply of the recovered substance.
The accused had criminal antecedents, including two previous cases registered under the NDPS Act.
The Public Prosecutor had opposed the grant of anticipatory bail in the High Court.
law: Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act imposes strict conditions for granting bail in cases involving commercial quantities of drugs.

If the Public Prosecutor opposes bail, the court must mandatorily record its satisfaction on two points: 1) there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty, and 2) the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
This stringent requirement applies to both regular and anticipatory bail.
Courts should be especially slow to grant bail, particularly anticipatory bail, in cases involving huge quantities of narcotics and an accused with a criminal history.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had completely ignored the fact that a massive quantity of narcotics was recovered.
The High Court also failed to consider the accused's criminal antecedents, specifically the prior NDPS Act cases.

Most importantly, the High Court failed to record the mandatory satisfaction required under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. It did not provide any reasoning to show it believed the accused was not guilty and would not re-offend.
The Supreme Court characterized the High Court's order as "cryptic and perverse on the face of the record" for its failure to apply the correct legal standard.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail was not justified because it failed to adhere to the mandatory conditions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act and ignored critical facts like the huge quantity of drugs and the accused's criminal history. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed and set aside the High Court's order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the filing of a charge-sheet against the accused after investigation fortifies the prosecution's case and weighs against the possibility of recording a satisfaction that the accused is prima facie not guilty.

facts: An investigation was conducted into offences under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) involving a commercial quantity of ganja.
Following the investigation, a charge-sheet was filed against the respondent-accused and others.
law: Under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, if the Public Prosecutor opposes a bail application for offences involving commercial quantities, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty of the offence.
This satisfaction must be recorded by the court before granting bail.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that a charge-sheet is filed only after an investigation has been completed.
The act of filing a charge-sheet indicates that the investigating agency has found sufficient material to proceed against the accused.
This strengthens, or "fortifies," the prosecution's argument that a prima facie case exists against the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the filing of a charge-sheet after an investigation fortifies the prosecution's case. This makes it difficult for a court to record the satisfaction required by Section 37 of the NDPS Act—that the accused is prima facie not guilty—and therefore weighs against the granting of bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether anticipatory bail can be granted in a case involving a commercial quantity of a narcotic substance without the court mandatorily recording the satisfaction required under Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
appellant_arguments: The State opposed the grant of anticipatory bail, and their plea, as fortified by the Supreme Court, was that the court could not have recorded a satisfaction that the accused was prima facie not guilty of the alleged offences, a mandatory condition for bail under the NDPS Act.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that he had not committed any offense, had been falsely implicated, and that other co-accused in the case had already been released on statutory bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail was justified, despite ignoring the recovery of a narcotic substance multiple times the commercial quantity and the alleged criminal antecedents of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The Additional Public Prosecutor, representing the State, vehemently opposed the grant of anticipatory bail by highlighting that there were 3 previous cases pending against the petitioner (accused).
respondent_arguments: The respondent claimed that the previous cases against him were fabricated ('put up cases') by the police in order to falsely implicate him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the filing of a charge-sheet against the accused after investigation fortifies the prosecution's case and weighs against the possibility of recording a satisfaction that the accused is prima facie not guilty.
appellant_arguments: The State argued that the fact that a charge-sheet has been filed against the accused after investigation strengthens the prosecution's case, making it untenable for a court to record a satisfaction that the accused is prima facie not guilty.
respondent_arguments: The respondent contended that since the investigation had concluded and a charge-sheet had been filed, the matter had progressed significantly, implying that his custody was no longer required for investigation.

statutes.act_name: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a Public Prosecutor opposes a bail application, the court must record its satisfaction that there are grounds for believing the accused is not guilty of the alleged offence and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
obiter: The fact that a charge-sheet has been filed against an accused fortifies the argument that a court could not have recorded a satisfaction that the accused was prima facie not guilty of the offences alleged.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's order granting anticipatory bail was cryptic, perverse, and unsustainable because it failed to adhere to the mandatory requirements of Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The High Court not only omitted to record the necessary satisfaction that there were reasonable grounds to believe the accused was not guilty and unlikely to re-offend, but it also completely ignored crucial facts against granting bail. These facts included the recovery of a narcotic substance multiple times the commercial quantity, the accused's criminal antecedents, and the subsequent filing of a charge-sheet which fortified the prosecution's case, making a finding of prima facie innocence untenable.
legal_tests_applied: For entertaining a prayer for bail in a case involving recovery of a commercial quantity of a narcotic drug, where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court must mandatorily record its satisfaction based on the twin conditions in Section 37 of the NDPS Act: (i) that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence, and (ii) that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
policy_considerations: In case of recovery of such a huge quantity of narcotic substance, the Courts should be slow in granting even regular bail to the accused what to talk of anticipatory bail more so when the accused is alleged to be having criminal antecedents.
